title: File sync (Dropbox / Google Drive)
tagline: Keep a folder identical on every device, moving only the 4 MB chunks that changed.
summary: Split the problem in two. Bytes: the client cuts each file into 4 MB chunks named by their SHA-256 hash and uploads only chunks the server has never seen, straight to object storage with presigned URLs. Metadata: a file version is just an ordered list of chunk hashes, committed in a SQL transaction that checks the version it was based on. Other devices hear 'something changed' through a long-poll, ask for changes since their cursor, and download only the chunks they lack. Conflicts are not merged: the loser becomes a conflicted copy.

functional: A folder stays in sync across a user's laptop, phone and the web
Upload and download files of any size; resume after a dropped connection
Edits made offline sync when the device reconnects
Version history: restore any version from the last 30 days
Two devices editing the same file never silently lose either edit
nonfunctional: Never lose or corrupt a file (object storage gives ~11 nines durability; you must not break it with bad metadata)
A change shows up on other online devices within a few seconds
Move as few bytes as possible: a 1-byte edit to a 1 GB file must not re-upload 1 GB
Scale to hundreds of petabytes and tens of millions of devices
out_of_scope: Real-time co-editing (that is a Google Docs design, with OT/CRDTs)

estimates.label: Upload bandwidth
estimates.calc: 50M changes × ~1 MB of new chunks per day

api.desc: Straight to object storage. Storage rejects bytes whose SHA-256 does not match.
200 {rev} on success; 409 {head_rev} if someone else committed first.
Journal entries after the cursor, paged: {entries[], cursor, has_more}.
Returns {changed: true} as soon as the namespace moves past the cursor, else times out.
302 to a short-lived presigned GET (or a CDN URL).

data.name: file_versions
data.note: A version is a list of hashes, so a new version of a 1 GB file is a few KB of metadata plus the changed chunks.

data.name: journal
data.note: Append-only change log per namespace. A device's whole sync state is one number: its cursor.

data.name: chunk_index
data.note: Answers 'do we have this chunk?' for dedupe, and drives garbage collection when refcount reaches 0.

data.name: chunks
data.note: Immutable. Same content, same key, so a chunk is never overwritten.

steps.note: You save a 40 MB spreadsheet. The client's file watcher sees it, cuts it into ten 4 MB chunks and hashes each with SHA-256. Only chunk 7 differs from rev 17. It sends all ten hashes.
POST /blocks/check: which of these hashes are new to you?
One batched lookup in the chunk index: 9 known, 1 new. Mark the new one pending and return a presigned PUT URL, valid ~15 min. Signing is a local HMAC; no call to storage.
The client PUTs 4 MB straight to object storage. Your servers never carry file bytes, so they scale with metadata, not bandwidth. A failed chunk is retried alone.
The block service confirms the object exists and its SHA-256 matches (the presigned PUT can require a checksum header). Only then is the chunk present. Never trust a client that says 'uploaded'.
POST /commit {path, parent_rev: 17, chunks[10]}.
Every listed chunk must be present; increment each one's refcount so garbage collection never deletes a chunk a version still uses.
One SQL transaction: check the file's head is still rev 17 (optimistic concurrency), insert rev 18 with its chunk list, append a journal row (cursor 9,001). If head moved, return 409: a conflict.
The client stores rev 18 as the base for its next edit. Bytes moved: 4 MB, not 40 MB.
The phone holds GET /notify?cursor=9000 open for up to ~60 s. Idle long-polls cost almost nothing, so one notify box holds a million. Dropbox's public API has the same shape (list_folder/longpoll).
After the commit, the metadata service publishes 'namespace 42 is at cursor 9,001'. It is only a signal, never file data, so it is tiny and safe to drop.
The long-poll returns {changed: true} at once. If the signal were lost, the poll times out and the phone checks anyway: the cursor makes it self-healing.
GET /changes?cursor=9000.
Routed to the metadata service for namespace 42's shard.
Read journal rows after 9000: 'spreadsheet.xlsx is now rev 18' with its chunk list. Paged, so a device that was offline for a month catches up in batches.
Return the entries and the new cursor 9,001. The phone compares the chunk list with what it already has: it lacks only chunk 7.
Download 4 MB through a presigned GET or CDN, verify the hash, write to a temp file and atomically rename. Phones often fetch lazily, only when the user opens the file.

flows.name: Dedupe hit
flows.desc: A 200 MB upload that moves zero bytes.

steps.note: You copy a 200 MB installer into the folder; 50 chunks, all hashed locally.
Ask which of the 50 hashes are new.
All 50 are already present (you uploaded the same file last month, in another folder). Nothing to upload.
Commit immediately with the 50 hashes.
Refcount +1 on each of the 50 chunks.
Insert the new file version pointing at existing chunks. The 'upload' finishes in under a second.
Other devices are notified as usual; they may already have those chunks locally too.

deep.title: Why 4 MB chunks, named by hash
deep.html:
• Resume: a dropped connection loses at most one chunk, not a 5 GB upload.
  • Parallel: upload 4-8 chunks at once to fill the pipe.
  • Delta: an edit re-uploads only the chunks whose hash changed.
  • Dedupe: the hash is the name, so identical content is stored once.

Fixed-size chunks have one weakness: insert one byte at the start of a file and every chunk boundary shifts, so every hash changes. Content-defined chunking (a rolling hash such as Rabin cuts where the content matches a pattern) keeps most boundaries in place. Use fixed 4 MB for simplicity and mention CDC as the upgrade. Smaller chunks dedupe better but mean more metadata: 62B chunks at 4 MB would be 250B at 1 MB.

deep.title: Conflicts: compare-and-set on the parent revision
deep.html: Every commit says which revision it was based on. The database accepts it only if that is still the head, in one transaction. The second writer gets 409. Its client does not merge (you cannot merge two edits of a spreadsheet blindly); it saves its version as report (Bob's conflicted copy 2026-11-19).xlsx and syncs that as a new file. Nothing is lost, and the person decides. Last-writer-wins would be simpler and would silently drop someone's work.

steps.note: The laptop reconnects first and commits with parent_rev 17.
Head is 17, so the update succeeds: head becomes rev 18.
Laptop gets 200 rev 18.
The phone commits its own edit, also based on 17.
WHERE rev = 17 matches zero rows: head is already 18.
409. The phone renames its version to a conflicted copy, commits that as a new file, then downloads rev 18. Both edits survive.

deep.title: Dedupe scope and garbage collection
deep.html:
Cross-user dedupe saves the most storage, but leaks information: if your 'upload' finishes instantly, you learn someone else already has that exact file. Many services dedupe only within a user or team, and dedupe is impossible across users if files are end-to-end encrypted with per-user keys.

Garbage collection: deleting a file only writes a new version. After the 30-day history window, an async job drops old versions and decrements chunk refcounts. A chunk at refcount 0 is deleted only after a grace period, because a client may be committing a version that reuses it right now.

deep.title: Notifications at scale
deep.html: Long-poll works through every corporate proxy and needs no special infrastructure; a WebSocket saves a reconnect per change. Either way, send only 'namespace N changed', never data, and let the device pull by cursor. The hard case is a team folder shared by 10,000 devices: one commit wakes all of them at once. Add 0-5 s of random jitter before they fetch, and cache the journal tail so 10,000 identical reads hit memory, not the database.

tradeoffs.choice: Send bytes through your servers or presigned URLs?
tradeoffs.why: At ~50 TB/day your app tier would be a bandwidth business. Presigned URLs let storage carry the bytes while your servers only sign and verify.
Simple and good for most edits that rewrite in place. CDC is better for inserts in big files and costs more CPU on the client.
Binary files cannot be merged safely and last-writer-wins loses work silently. A visible extra file is annoying but never destructive.
A commit must check the head revision, insert a version and append to the journal atomically. One namespace per shard keeps that a single-shard transaction.

tradeoffs.choice: Long-poll or WebSocket for change signals?
tradeoffs.why: Works everywhere, stateless to load-balance, and changes are infrequent per device. Switch to WebSocket if you add live collaboration.

bottlenecks.issue: A 10,000-device team folder: one change triggers 10,000 fetches
bottlenecks.fix: Jitter the fetch, cache the journal tail in memory, and page the changes response.

bottlenecks.issue: A new laptop syncs a 500,000-file account
bottlenecks.fix: Page the journal from cursor 0, download metadata first and file contents lazily or by priority (recent and small files first).

bottlenecks.issue: One huge namespace outgrows its shard
bottlenecks.fix: Give very large namespaces a dedicated shard; the journal cursor stays per namespace, so devices do not notice.

followups.q: How do you restore a file deleted two weeks ago?
followups.a: Deleting wrote a new version with deleted = true. The old version row still lists its chunk hashes, and their refcounts kept the chunks alive. Restore = commit a new version with that old chunk list.

followups.q: How do you upload a 50 GB video over a flaky connection?
followups.a: 12,500 chunks, uploaded 4-8 in parallel, each retried on its own. Progress is just 'which hashes are present', so after a crash the client asks /blocks/check again and continues. Commit once at the end.

followups.q: Someone inserts one byte at the start of a 1 GB file. What happens?
followups.a: With fixed chunks, every boundary shifts and all 250 chunks re-upload. Content-defined chunking cuts at content patterns, so only the first chunk changes. That is the main argument for CDC.

followups.q: How do you keep chunks safe from other users?
followups.a: Chunks are only reachable through short-lived presigned URLs, which the server signs only for chunks in versions you can read. Storage is encrypted at rest, and the block service must check access before handing out a GET URL.

quiz.q: Why upload chunks with presigned URLs instead of through the API servers?
options: Presigned URLs are encrypted and the API isn't
Object storage carries the bytes, so the API tier only handles small metadata requests
quiz.why: At tens of TB a day, keeping bytes off the app tier is what lets it scale.

quiz.q: Two devices both commit edits based on rev 17. What does the second one get?
options: Its edit silently overwrites the first
A 409, and its client saves a conflicted copy
quiz.why: Compare-and-set on the parent revision detects the conflict; the conflicted copy keeps both edits.

quiz.q: What is a device's entire sync state on the server side?
options: A full list of its files
Its cursor into the namespace's change journal
quiz.why: Ask for 'changes after cursor N' and you get everything you missed, in order.

quiz.q: Why must garbage collection wait before deleting a chunk whose refcount hit 0?
options: A client may be committing a new version that reuses that chunk right now
quiz.why: Dedupe means a chunk can gain a new reference at any moment; the grace period closes that race.

quiz.q: Which change makes fixed-size chunking re-upload almost the whole file?
options: Changing one byte in the middle
quiz.why: An insert shifts every later chunk boundary. Content-defined chunking avoids this.
